title: MAE vs MSE vs RMSE vs R²
tagline: Four ways to measure how wrong your model is — and why it matters which one you pick.
what_it_is: These are regression error metrics — numbers that tell you how far off your model's predictions are from reality. MAE (Mean Absolute Error) is the average gap between predicted and actual values. MSE (Mean Squared Error) squares those gaps before averaging, punishing large errors more harshly. RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error) is just MSE square-rooted back to the original unit. R² (R-squared) tells you what percentage of the variation in your data your model actually explains.
why_it_exists: A model that predicts house prices can be wrong in many different ways — slightly wrong on most houses, or catastrophically wrong on a few. These metrics exist because different use cases care about different types of wrongness. A metric that treats all errors equally (MAE) is right for some problems. A metric that punishes large mistakes extra hard (MSE/RMSE) is right for others. Without these measures, you have no objective way to compare two models or know if your model is good enough.
what_it_measures: Each metric measures a different aspect of prediction error. MAE measures the typical size of your errors in plain units — dollars, degrees, kilograms. MSE measures the same but amplifies large errors so they dominate the score. RMSE brings MSE back to interpretable units. R² measures not the size of your errors but how much better your model is than simply predicting the mean every time — a score of 1.0 is perfect, 0.0 means your model adds no value over a naive guess.
intuition: Imagine you are a weather forecaster. On Monday you are off by 2°, Tuesday by 3°, Wednesday by 10° (you missed a storm completely). MAE treats all three days equally — average error is 5°. MSE punishes Wednesday's disaster: 4 + 9 + 100 = 113, averaged to 37.7. RMSE brings that back to degrees: √37.7 = 6.1°. The big miss on Wednesday inflates your RMSE far above your MAE. That difference is the signal — RMSE tells you that you have an outlier problem, MAE hides it.

when_to_use: Use MAE when all prediction errors matter equally and you want a result in the same unit as your target — easy to explain to non-technical stakeholders
Use MSE/RMSE when large errors are especially dangerous — medical dosing, structural load predictions, financial risk — because it penalises outlier mistakes heavily
Use RMSE over MSE when you need the error in the original unit (MSE gives squared units which are uninterpretable)
Use R² when comparing two models on the same dataset — it tells you which explains more of the variance
Use R² alongside MAE or RMSE together — R² alone does not tell you the actual size of your errors
when_not_to_use: Do not use R² as your only metric — high R² does not mean small errors, it means your model tracks the pattern. You can have R²=0.95 and still have errors too large to be useful
Do not use MSE to report results to stakeholders — squared units (e.g. dollars²) are meaningless to humans, use RMSE or MAE instead
Do not use MAE when large individual errors are catastrophic — it will make a model with occasional disasters look acceptable
Do not compare R² across different datasets or target variables — it is a relative measure and loses meaning across different problems
Do not use any of these for classification problems — they are regression-only, use accuracy, F1, AUC instead
common_mistakes: Reporting R²=0.87 and declaring the model good without checking actual error size — you need MAE or RMSE to know if errors are acceptable for your use case
Comparing MAE from one model to RMSE from another — they are not on the same scale, the comparison is meaningless
Using MSE to compare models trained on datasets of different scales — wildly different MSE values will be unrelated to actual model quality
Ignoring that RMSE is always >= MAE — the gap between them tells you how much large errors are hurting you, a big gap means an outlier problem worth investigating
ds_usage: These metrics appear at the end of every regression model evaluation pipeline. In scikit-learn: mean_absolute_error(), mean_squared_error(), r2_score() from sklearn.metrics. In practice you compute all four, report MAE or RMSE to stakeholders, and use the MAE-RMSE gap to detect outlier sensitivity. When tuning models via cross-validation, the choice of which metric to optimise directly shapes what the model learns to minimise — choose carefully.
key_points: MAE = average absolute error. Treats all errors equally. Interpretable unit. Use for general reporting.
MSE = average squared error. Punishes large mistakes hard. Uninterpretable squared unit. Use for training loss.
RMSE = √MSE. Same penalty as MSE but back in original unit. Best choice for reporting to humans.
R² = proportion of variance explained. 1.0 is perfect, 0.0 is no better than always guessing the mean.
The gap between MAE and RMSE is diagnostic — a large gap means a few big errors are dominating your score.
